_schema.d: discovery: [year (negative = BCE; earliest known use for ancient elements), discoverers, place, lat, lon, method, note]
_schema.method: ancient | chemical | electrolysis | mineral | gas | spectroscopy | xray | radiochemistry | synthesis | debris
_schema.bio: [role, note] — role: bulk | trace | beneficial | none | toxic | radioactive (human / organism biology)
_schema.mag: [ordering at ~298 K: dia | para | ferro | antiferro | unknown, optional note on low-temperature ordering]

d: Collected 'inflammable air' from metals in acid and showed it burned to water; Lavoisier named it hydrogène (1783).
bio: ~10% of body mass; in water and every organic molecule; proton gradients drive ATP synthesis.

d: A yellow D3 line in the solar prominence spectrum matched no known element; Ramsay isolated it on Earth from cleveite (London, 1895).
bio: Inert; inhaled only as a diluent (heliox) or asphyxiant.

d: Found while analysing petalite from Utö; Brande and Davy isolated the metal by electrolysis (1821).
bio: No known essential role; lithium salts are a frontline mood-stabilising drug.

d: Identified a new oxide in beryl and emerald; Wöhler and Bussy isolated the metal (1828).
bio: Inhaled dust causes chronic beryllium disease (berylliosis); carcinogen.

d: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac & Louis Jacques Thénard; Humphry Davy
Reduced boric acid with potassium; Davy did the same independently in London days later.
bio: Essential for plants (cell walls); probably beneficial for bone in humans.

d: Charcoal reduced copper ores in early smelting; Lavoisier listed carbon as an element (1789), Tennant showed diamond is pure carbon (1797).
bio: Backbone of all organic molecules; ~18% of body mass.

d: Isolated the 'noxious air' left after burning and absorbing carbon dioxide; Scheele, Cavendish and Priestley worked on it in parallel.
bio: In every amino acid and nucleotide; ~3% of body mass.

d: Priestley heated mercuric oxide (1774); Scheele had prepared it in Uppsala c. 1771 but published later; Lavoisier explained combustion with it.
bio: Terminal electron acceptor of respiration; ~65% of body mass.
mag: Paramagnetic O2 (two unpaired electrons) — liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet; solid O2 antiferromagnetic below 24 K.

d: Electrolysed KHF2 dissolved in anhydrous HF at about −23 °C after 74 years of failed attempts (Nobel Prize 1906); Ampère proposed the element in 1810.
bio: Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel (fluorapatite); F2 and HF are acutely toxic.

d: Fractional distillation of liquefied air at University College London; its crimson discharge glow gave it away.
Electrolysed molten caustic soda (NaOH) at the Royal Institution days after isolating potassium.
bio: Main extracellular cation; drives nerve impulses via the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

d: Black distinguished magnesia from lime in Edinburgh (1755); Davy isolated an amalgam of the metal; Bussy made it pure in 1831.
bio: Centre of chlorophyll; cofactor for >300 enzymes and every ATP reaction.

d: Reduced AlCl3 with potassium amalgam; Wöhler made purer metal (1827); the Hall–Héroult electrolysis (1886) made it cheap.
bio: No known role; poorly absorbed; neurotoxic at high exposure (dialysis).

d: Reduced potassium fluorosilicate with potassium and purified the amorphous product.
bio: Structural in diatoms, sponges and grasses; possibly beneficial for human bone and connective tissue.

d: Boiled down and distilled ~5,000 L of urine looking for the philosopher's stone — the first element discovered by a named individual.
bio: Phosphate backbone of DNA/RNA, ATP energy currency, bone mineral (hydroxyapatite).

d: Ancient Chinese, Indian and Mediterranean cultures
Burned as a fumigant and used in medicine and gunpowder (9th c. China); Lavoisier proved it an element (1777).
bio: In cysteine and methionine; disulfide bridges fold proteins; iron–sulfur clusters.

d: Reacted pyrolusite (MnO2) with hydrochloric acid; Davy proved it an element and named it (1810).
Nitrogen extracted from air was 0.5% denser than chemically produced nitrogen — the excess was an unknown inert gas.
Electrolysed molten potash (KOH) — the first metal isolated by electrolysis.
bio: Main intracellular cation; sets the membrane resting potential.

d: Electrolysed a mixture of lime and mercuric oxide to form an amalgam, then distilled off the mercury.
bio: Bones and teeth; universal intracellular signal for muscle contraction and secretion.

d: Found in euxenite and gadolinite — Mendeleev's predicted eka-boron, confirmed by Cleve.
Found in black ilmenite sand ('menachanite'); Klaproth named it (1795); the Kroll process (1940) made the metal practical.
bio: Biologically inert — ideal for implants; TiO2 nanoparticles under study.

d: Found it in 'brown lead' (vanadinite) but was persuaded it was chromium; Sefström rediscovered and named it (Falun, 1830).
bio: Cofactor in some nitrogenases and haloperoxidases; sea squirts concentrate it.

d: Isolated from crocoite ('Siberian red lead'); named for its many colourful compounds.
bio: Cr(III) long considered essential for glucose metabolism (now debated); Cr(VI) is a carcinogen.
mag: Antiferromagnetic below its Néel temperature of 311 K (spin-density wave).

d: Johan Gottlieb Gahn (with Scheele and Bergman)
Gahn reduced pyrolusite with charcoal; Scheele had recognised the new element in the ore.
bio: Heart of the photosynthetic water-splitting complex; cofactor of superoxide dismutase.

d: Meteoric iron beads c. 3500 BCE; bloomery smelting spread from Anatolia c. 1200 BCE, opening the Iron Age.
bio: Oxygen transport in haemoglobin; cytochromes; the most abundant trace metal in the body.

d: Showed the blue colour of smalt glass came from a new metal rather than bismuth; named after kobold, the mine goblin.
mag: Ferromagnetic; highest Curie temperature of any element, 1388 K.

d: Isolated from niccolite, the 'Kupfernickel' (copper-demon) ore that yielded no copper.
bio: Essential for plants (urease) and many microbes; common contact allergen in humans.

d: Neolithic peoples of the Middle East
A copper pendant from northern Iraq dates to c. 8700 BCE; smelting from ore appears by c. 5000 BCE.
bio: Electron transfer in cytochrome c oxidase; haemocyanin carries oxygen in molluscs.

d: Indian metallurgists (Zawar); Andreas Marggraf in Europe (1746)
Distilled at Zawar from about the 9th century CE in retort furnaces; Marggraf isolated it independently in Berlin (1746).
bio: Structural/catalytic in >300 enzymes and zinc-finger transcription factors.

d: Two violet lines in a zinc-blende spectrum — Mendeleev's predicted eka-aluminium.
bio: No known role; gallium compounds used in imaging and as drugs.

d: Isolated from argyrodite — Mendeleev's eka-silicon, whose predicted properties matched closely.
Heated orpiment with soap to obtain the element; arsenic sulfides were used since antiquity.
bio: Potent poison and carcinogen; a few microbes respire arsenate.

d: Jöns Jacob Berzelius & Johan Gottlieb Gahn
Found in red sludge from a sulfuric acid works at Gripsholm; named after the Moon (selene) as tellurium's sibling.
bio: In selenocysteine (glutathione peroxidase, thyroid deiodinases); narrow window between deficiency and toxicity.

d: Extracted from salt-marsh brine with chlorine; Carl Löwig isolated it independently in Heidelberg.
bio: Required for collagen IV scaffolds in animal tissue (2014 finding); Br2 is corrosive.

d: Residue left after evaporating liquefied air.
Two deep-red spectral lines in lepidolite (rubidus = deep red).
bio: No known role; behaves like potassium in the body.

d: Recognised in strontianite from Strontian, Scotland; Davy isolated the metal by electrolysis (1808).
bio: Substitutes for calcium in bone; radioactive Sr-90 is a fallout hazard.

d: Isolated 'yttria' from a black mineral (gadolinite) found at Ytterby, Sweden.
Found zirconia in zircon from Sri Lanka; Berzelius isolated the metal (1824).
bio: No known role; low toxicity, used in implants.

d: Found in a columbite sample from Connecticut and named it columbium; Heinrich Rose separated it from tantalum (1844).
mag: Superconducting below 9.25 K — the highest Tc of any element at ambient pressure.

d: Carl Wilhelm Scheele (isolated by Peter Jacob Hjelm, 1781)
Showed molybdenite was not graphite or lead ore; Hjelm reduced the oxide with carbon.
bio: In the molybdopterin cofactor of nitrogenase, xanthine oxidase and sulfite oxidase.

d: Found in molybdenum foil irradiated in Lawrence's Berkeley cyclotron — the first artificially produced element.
bio: No role; Tc-99m is the most used medical radiotracer in the world.

d: Extracted from residues of Ural platinum ore; named for Ruthenia (Russia).
Isolated from platinum ore dissolved in aqua regia; named for its rose-red salts.
Separated from crude platinum; named after the newly found asteroid Pallas.
Cupellation of argentiferous lead ores c. 3000 BCE produced the first silver in quantity.
bio: No role; antimicrobial; argyria from chronic ingestion.

d: Found as an impurity colouring zinc carbonate yellow when heated.
bio: Accumulates in kidneys, causes itai-itai disease; one marine diatom uses it in carbonic anhydrase.

d: An indigo-blue line appeared in the spectrum of zinc ore; the colour-blind Reich needed Richter to see it.
Alloyed with copper to make bronze c. 3500 BCE; tin was traded from Anatolia, Iran and later Cornwall.
bio: Inorganic tin has low toxicity; organotins are highly toxic.

d: A vase fragment of antimony from Tello dates to c. 3000 BCE; stibnite was used as kohl eye cosmetic.
bio: Toxic like arsenic; antimonials are used against leishmaniasis.

d: Found in Transylvanian gold ore; Klaproth confirmed and named it (1798).
bio: No role; exposure gives a garlic odour to breath.

d: Violet vapour rose from seaweed ash treated with sulfuric acid in a saltpetre works; Gay-Lussac named it.
bio: Essential for thyroid hormones T3 and T4; heaviest element needed by humans.

d: The last, heaviest residue of liquid-air distillation; Bartlett made the first noble-gas compound with it (1962).
bio: Inert but anaesthetic at high partial pressure.

d: Two sky-blue lines in Dürkheim mineral water — the first element found with the spectroscope.
bio: No role; Cs-137 is a major fission-product hazard.

d: Humphry Davy (Carl Wilhelm Scheele recognised baryta, 1772)
Scheele distinguished baryta from lime; Davy isolated the metal by electrolysis of molten salts.
bio: Soluble salts are poisonous (K⁺ channel block); insoluble BaSO4 is a safe X-ray contrast agent.

d: Found 'hiding' in cerium oxide (lanthanein = to lie hidden).
bio: Used by methanotrophic bacteria in methanol dehydrogenase; La carbonate is a phosphate binder.

d: Jöns Jacob Berzelius & Wilhelm Hisinger; Martin Klaproth
Found in cerite from Bastnäs; named after the asteroid Ceres.
bio: Used by some methanotrophic bacteria; no human role.

d: Split 'didymium' into praseodymium (green twin) and neodymium by repeated fractional crystallisation.

mag: Antiferromagnetic below ~19 K; Nd2Fe14B is the strongest permanent magnet.

d: Jacob Marinsky, Lawrence Glendenin & Charles Coryell
Identified by ion-exchange chromatography of uranium fission products from the Clinton reactor.
Separated from samarskite — the first element named (indirectly) after a person, Col. Samarsky.
mag: Antiferromagnetic below ~14 K; SmCo5 is a high-temperature permanent magnet.

d: Separated from samarium–gadolinium concentrates and confirmed by its spectrum.
Observed spectroscopic lines in didymium and gadolinite; Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated the oxide (1886).
bio: No role; free Gd³⁺ is toxic, chelated Gd is an MRI contrast agent.
mag: Ferromagnetic only below its Curie temperature of 293 K (≈20 °C) — paramagnetic on a warm day.

d: Separated from yttria along with erbium.
mag: Ferromagnetic below 219 K; Terfenol-D shows giant magnetostriction.

d: Separated from holmium after more than 30 attempts — dysprositos = hard to get at.
mag: Antiferromagnetic below 179 K, ferromagnetic below 85 K.

d: Marc Delafontaine & Jacques-Louis Soret; Per Teodor Cleve (1879)
Spectroscopic lines in erbia; Cleve isolated the oxide in Uppsala and named it after Stockholm (Holmia).
mag: Highest magnetic moment of any element; orders below 132 K.

d: Separated from yttria; named after Ytterby.
mag: Antiferromagnetic below 85 K, ferromagnetic below ~20 K.

d: Separated from erbia; named after Thule, the mythical far north.
Separated from erbia by thermal decomposition of nitrates.
Georges Urbain (also Carl Auer von Welsbach, Charles James)
Separated from ytterbia; named after Lutetia, Latin for Paris.
bio: No role; Lu-177 is used in targeted cancer radiotherapy.

d: Found by X-ray spectroscopy in Norwegian zircon at Bohr's institute, as Bohr's theory predicted (not a rare earth).
Found in tantalite; named after Tantalus because the oxide would not dissolve ('drink') in acid.
Reduced tungstic acid from wolframite with charcoal; Scheele had obtained tungstic acid from scheelite (1781).
bio: Cofactor in enzymes of some archaea and bacteria — the heaviest element with a biological role.

d: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke & Otto Berg
Detected by X-ray spectroscopy in gadolinite and platinum ores; the last stable element discovered.
Found in the black residue of platinum dissolved in aqua regia; named for the smell (osme) of OsO4.
bio: OsO4 is volatile and highly toxic to eyes and lungs.

d: Isolated alongside osmium; named for the rainbow (Iris) of its salts' colours.
Antonio de Ulloa (pre-Columbian South Americans worked it earlier)
Ulloa described 'platina' (little silver) from Colombian gold mines; pre-Columbian smiths sintered it with gold.
bio: No role; cisplatin and carboplatin are major anticancer drugs.

d: The Varna necropolis holds the oldest worked gold, c. 4500 BCE.
bio: No role; gold salts once used for rheumatoid arthritis.

d: Found in Egyptian tombs c. 1500 BCE; cinnabar was roasted to mercury in China and the Mediterranean.
bio: Neurotoxin, especially methylmercury bioaccumulated in fish.

d: A bright green line in residues from a sulfuric acid plant (thallos = green shoot).
Lead beads at Çatalhöyük date to c. 6500 BCE; Romans used it for plumbing (plumbum).
bio: Cumulative neurotoxin; no safe blood level in children.

d: Proved distinct from lead and tin; miners in the 1400s already knew 'wismuth'.
bio: Low toxicity for a heavy metal; bismuth subsalicylate treats ulcers and diarrhoea.
mag: The most strongly diamagnetic element — it levitates over strong magnets.

d: Chemically separated from pitchblende by following its radioactivity; named after Marie's homeland, Poland.
bio: Po-210 is an intense alpha emitter — lethal in microgram amounts if ingested.

d: Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie & Emilio Segrè
Bombarded bismuth-209 with alpha particles in the 60-inch cyclotron; natural astatine was found later in decay chains.
bio: No role; At-211 under study for targeted alpha therapy.

d: Observed a radioactive gas ('emanation') given off by radium compounds; Ramsay and Gray measured its density (1910).
bio: Second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking (indoor radon).

d: Found as a decay product of actinium-227 at the Curie Institute — the last element discovered in nature.
bio: No role; half-life of only 22 minutes.

d: Separated from tonnes of pitchblende; Marie Curie and Debierne isolated the metal (1910).
bio: Bone-seeking (calcium mimic); caused the 'Radium Girls' tragedy; Ra-223 treats bone metastases.

d: Found in pitchblende residues left by the Curies; Giesel discovered it independently (1902).
bio: No role; Ac-225 is used in targeted alpha therapy.

d: Identified in thorite found on Løvøya, Norway; named after Thor.
bio: No role; weakly radioactive alpha emitter.

d: Found the short-lived isotope Pa-234m; Hahn and Meitner (Berlin) and Soddy and Cranston found long-lived Pa-231 (1917–18).
bio: No role; highly toxic alpha emitter.

d: Found in pitchblende and named after the planet Uranus; Péligot isolated the metal (1841); Becquerel found radioactivity in it (1896).
Neutron-irradiated uranium in the Berkeley cyclotron — the first transuranium element.
Glenn Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy & Arthur Wahl
Deuteron bombardment of uranium-238 in the 60-inch cyclotron; kept secret until 1946.
bio: Bone- and liver-seeking alpha emitter; a severe inhalation hazard.

d: Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan & Albert Ghiorso
Made by successive neutron capture in plutonium at the wartime Met Lab; Am-241 now sits in smoke detectors.
Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James & Albert Ghiorso
Alpha bombardment of Pu-239 at Berkeley, identified at Chicago; named for Marie and Pierre Curie.
Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso & Glenn Seaborg
Stanley Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso & Glenn Seaborg
Alpha bombardment of curium-242; Cf-252 is a compact neutron source.
Albert Ghiorso et al. (Berkeley, Argonne, Los Alamos)
Enewetak Atoll, Marshall Islands (Ivy Mike test)
Found in debris from the first hydrogen-bomb test, where U-238 captured up to 15 neutrons; classified until 1955.
Albert Ghiorso et al. (Berkeley, Argonne, Los Alamos)
Enewetak Atoll, Marshall Islands (Ivy Mike test)
Also found in Ivy Mike fallout; the heaviest element that can be made by neutron capture.
Albert Ghiorso, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin, Stanley Thompson & Glenn Seaborg
Identified from just 17 atoms made by alpha bombardment of einsteinium-253.
Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (Georgy Flerov et al.)
Contested claims from Stockholm (1957) and Berkeley (1958); IUPAC credited Dubna's 1966 work.
Albert Ghiorso, Torbjørn Sikkeland, Almon Larsh & Robert Latimer
Boron ions on californium; credit shared with Dubna.
Cold-war naming dispute (kurchatovium vs rutherfordium) settled by IUPAC in 1997.
Credit shared; named after Dubna in 1997.
Oxygen-18 on californium-249; named for Glenn Seaborg while he was alive.
Cold fusion of chromium-54 with bismuth-209.
Iron-58 on lead-208; named after the German state of Hesse.
A single atom from iron-58 on bismuth-209; named for Lise Meitner.
Nickel-64 on bismuth-209; named for Wilhelm Röntgen.
Zinc-70 on lead-208; named for Copernicus.
Zinc-70 on bismuth-209 — three atoms in nine years; the first element named in Asia (Nihon = Japan).
JINR Dubna & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
Calcium-48 on plutonium-244; named after the Flerov Laboratory.
JINR Dubna & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
Calcium-48 on americium-243; named after the Moscow region.
JINR Dubna & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
Calcium-48 on curium-248; named after Livermore.
JINR Dubna, Oak Ridge NL, Vanderbilt & LLNL
Calcium-48 on berkelium-249 made at Oak Ridge; named after Tennessee.
JINR Dubna & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
Calcium-48 on californium-249 (announced 2006); named for Yuri Oganessian — the heaviest known element.
